cards.title: Avatar discovery via review mining
cards.summary: Mine competitor, marketplace and own-product reviews for identity phrases to uncover hidden buyer segments.
cards.use_when: You are picking a product to sell or launching a brand and need to identify which distinct buyer groups already buy something like it.
steps: Identify comparable products: if selling generic running shoes, look at reviews for Nike, Reebok, Under Armour and On Cloud because they sell into the same category.
Read reviews on generic marketplaces (e.g. AliExpress), competitor sites, and your own product reviews.

Scan for identity-marking phrases such as 'I am a…', 'As a…', or any phrasing where the reviewer explains who they are. Examples: 'I am a nurse, I'm on my feet all day and these On Clouds are amazing' or 'As a registered dietitian for the last 20 years I'm on my feet all day talking to patients'.
Tally recurring roles: a repeated 'as a nurse' pattern is a signal that a distinct avatar exists and is buying.
Use the discovered role as the basis for tailoring creative, product copy and product page later; note that downstream application happens in other modules.
caveats: Works best when there is enough review volume; a brand-new product with no reviews must rely on competitor and marketplace reviews.
Do not present the source's anecdotal volume claims as benchmarks.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Survey existing buyers to name your avatar
cards.summary: Use a free form and email to ask customers how they describe themselves, their situation and how the product helps.
cards.use_when: You have an existing customer list and want to turn implicit buyer segments into explicitly named avatars.
steps: Create a free Google Forms survey (verify current free limits and question types in the tool).
Send it to existing customers through whatever email software you already use.
Ask how they would describe themselves — role, job, family role (husband, father, wife) — and their specific job title.
Ask what specifically about the product works for them and what their unique situation is.
Look for answers that pair an identity with a mechanism, e.g. 'I'm a nurse, I'm on my feet all day, so these shoes work really well.'
Aggregate recurring identity-plus-situation pairs and treat those as avatar candidates.
caveats: The source positions this as baseline avatar discovery rather than an advanced method.
Self-reported descriptions can be aspirational; prefer patterns repeated across many respondents.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Talk to customers directly to detect your dominant avatar
cards.summary: One-on-one and group conversations reveal which avatar actually dominates your customer base.
cards.use_when: You already sell to a mixed audience and want to know which single avatar deserves concentrated messaging.
steps: Hold one-on-one and group calls with customers, as the source does inside a mentorship community.
Note the identity customers use when describing themselves, such as 'ecom brand owner'.
If roughly 95% of people in your program say they are ecom brand owners, treat ecom as the dominant avatar.
Point all outward content — Instagram, YouTube, landing page VSL, group call recordings — at that dominant avatar.
Re-run this periodically; if the mix shifts, the avatar the content should target shifts with it.
caveats: The 95% figure is the source's own program, not a general benchmark.
A dominant avatar in your existing base does not guarantee it is the largest available market; combine with review and trend research.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Market sophistication forces broad markets to fracture into sub-avatars
cards.summary: As buyers try and fail with generic offers, they demand specialists, creating niche avatar opportunities.
cards.use_when: You are choosing whether to address a whole market or a specialist slice of it, and need a reason to niche down.
steps: Recognise the sophistication curve: early buyers accept generic providers ('you run Facebook ads? run mine'), later buyers ask 'have you done this before?' and then 'I want someone who only works with my type of business'.

Note that this shift happened in agency markets around 2017–2018 when specialists for chiropractors, lawyers, dentists and roofers emerged after those buyers had already failed with generalist agencies.
Treat the resulting specialist niche as the avatar: a dialed-in subset of the broad market.

Accept that a niche can still be large enough to build a substantial business — the source cites a client agency serving only financial advisors that sold for roughly $3 million, though this is one example, not a target.
Prefer being narrow and deep over broad and shallow: with one avatar, systems, marketing and advertising can be fine-tuned and the message sharpened.
caveats: Not every market has reached this sophistication stage; specialisation is the growth move gated by market maturity.
The agency-sale figure is an anecdote, not a valuation benchmark for ecommerce.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Test whether a niche is big enough before specialising
cards.summary: Sub-niches can be too small to sustain a business, so check the size of the parent market before niching down.
cards.use_when: You have identified a sub-avatar and must decide whether to build a brand or offer exclusively for it.
steps: Estimate the size of the parent market first; the source notes gym-goers alone may exceed 100 million people worldwide, leaving room for many sub-niches.
Then estimate the sub-avatar. If the parent market is only around 20,000 people, a further sub-niche could contain just 100–1,000 people, which may be too small to promote into.

Check trend signals before committing: the founder of Gym Shark reportedly observed growing workout content online, then flew creators to an expo and sponsored them with clothing, which helped establish the gym-clothing niche.
Choose the depth of niching based on both the size of the parent market and the level of market sophistication.
caveats: Population estimates in the source are illustrative, not measured data.
The Gym Shark example is a case study, not a repeatable guarantee.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Map sub-avatars through social content
cards.summary: Watch how general niches split into distinct subcultures on TikTok and similar platforms.
cards.use_when: You want to find or anticipate emergent buyer subcultures inside a category you already understand.
steps: Search broad category terms on social platforms — e.g. bodybuilding, CrossFit, or gym clothing — and study the distinct groups posting.
Trace the nesting-doll split: mass athletic apparel (Reebok, Under Armour) served all sports and general gym-goers; Gym Shark then specialised in gym wear; further brands each claimed a sub-avatar.

Identify what distinguishes each sub-avatar, e.g. Anaka Power described as alternative, trend-resistant 'misfits'; Alphalite oriented around entrepreneur/learn-more-be-more values; Buff Bunny exclusively female; Young LA the 'broccoli-haired' gym-bench-scroll crowd.
Note the mechanisms brands use to signal the avatar: creatives, product design, branding, and which people they 'uplift' by featuring and sponsoring them.
Pick a sub-avatar whose identity you can signal consistently across all of these.
caveats: Brand characterisations reflect the source's own reading of these brands; verify current positioning before borrowing it.
Requires ongoing monitoring, since sub-avatars keep splitting.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Define an avatar by growth signals, not a definition
cards.summary: Treat an avatar as a group that is measurably growing in your reviews, customer base or community.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether an observed segment is a real avatar worth building around or just noise.
steps: Look for repetition: many reviews saying 'as a nurse' repeatedly, or many program joiners saying they are ecom owners.
Go one level deeper when a pattern holds — e.g. ecom owners who all do at least $100k a month, not just ecom owners.
Treat a rising count of people self-identifying the same way as the signal that the avatar is forming and growing.
Recognise the window: once a collective group gathers, they are waiting for someone to sell them something, so being first to serve them matters.
Keep re-checking; nested sub-avatars keep emerging, as the source says is currently happening with perimenopausal and postmenopausal weight-loss audiences spawning further subsets.
caveats: The source explicitly says there is no single-word definition of an avatar.
The $100k/month and menopause examples are the source's illustrations of the depth rule, not fixed thresholds.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Enter emerging trends as the first dedicated brand
cards.summary: When a new pastime takes off, sell into it as the first brand dedicated to participants rather than competing on the core equipment.
cards.use_when: You spot a fast-growing recreational trend and want a lower-competition entry point than the obvious product category.
steps: Identify an emerging trend or sport — the source uses cornhole becoming a mainstream sport in the USA.
Avoid the crowded core: do not try to compete with every cornhole board manufacturer.
Instead become the first dedicated brand for cornhole participants in an adjacent category: clothing, supplements, or an energy drink for cornhole players.
You can start from products that already exist in other niches and rebrand them as specifically for that avatar, with all marketing and advertising created only for that group.
Move early, since the advantage comes from being first to serve the newly forming avatar.
caveats: The cornhole example is the source's hypothetical illustration, not a documented launch result.
Emerging trends can fade; the source offers no validation criteria beyond early adoption.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: How deep niching fits ecommerce and dropshipping
cards.summary: The same avatar structure translates from agency niches to ecom brands by pointing a mass-market play at one sub-avatar.
cards.use_when: You are an ecommerce or dropshipping operator considering whether avatar specialisation applies to your model.
steps: Start with a mass-market product already proven by other ecom brands in a category.
Study the working ads of the mass-market brands and note what they claim and show.
Rework that same material for a single specific avatar instead of the whole market.
Tailor the primary text, the creative itself, the landing or product page, and even the way you name the business.
Only show results or case studies belonging to that avatar; generic proof undermines the fit.

The source describes a student who launched with a 5x ROAS on day one, then found the main buyers in his niche and copied competitors' mass-market ads while showing the result only for that avatar — an example, not a promised outcome.
caveats: The 5x-ROAS launch is a single anecdote and should not be treated as an expectation.
Copying competitor ads is only the starting point; the avatar-specific adaptation is the actual work.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Tailor the whole funnel to one avatar, not just the hook
cards.summary: Avatar fit must run through creative, primary text, page, proof and sales conversation — putting the avatar only in the hook is the common mistake.
cards.use_when: You have chosen an avatar and are rebuilding ads and landing/product pages to match it.
steps: Take the mass-market version of the message and adapt every layer: 'how to scale Facebook ads' becomes 'how to scale Facebook ads for roofers'.
Change the creative setting to match the avatar's world — the source's example goes from an office to standing on a roof.
Replace generic case studies on the landing page with only case studies belonging to that avatar (roofing results, not mixed results).
Adapt the sales conversation so it speaks to how the offer is tailored to that avatar's business.
Extend the same tailoring to product photos and every claim on the product page, framed by what that avatar wants.

The test: if someone outside the avatar lands in the funnel, they should feel they are in the wrong place. The source's analogy is ordering McDonald's and arriving at Chick-fil-A — the wrong-fit buyer should leave.
caveats: Deliberately repelling non-avatar traffic is the source's opinion, presented as a trade-off against trying to reach everyone.
It still runs on broad targeting; the creative, not the targeting settings, does the filtering.
Paid targeting structure belongs to a separate advertising module.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Keep broad targeting while narrowing the avatar
cards.summary: Pair avatar-specific creative with broad targeting and let Facebook's algorithm locate the matching audience.
cards.use_when: You are running Meta ads for a niche avatar and deciding whether to narrow the audience settings.
steps: Keep broad targeting even after niching down; the source states this is still what he does.
Let the platform do the audience-finding work based on which creatives perform.
Because the algorithm relies on the creative to find the right people, the creatives must be tightly dialed to the avatar.
Treat avatar-specific creative as the replacement for narrow audience settings, not an addition to them.
caveats: This is the source's stated practice; account structure and targeting settings are covered in another module and platform behaviour may change — verify current ad platform guidance.
Weak or generic creative under broad targeting gives the algorithm no avatar signal to work with.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx

cards.title: Rebrand existing products for a single avatar
cards.summary: Take products that already exist in other niches and market them exclusively to one avatar.
cards.use_when: You want to serve a newly forming avatar without developing new products from scratch.
steps: Identify the avatar first through reviews, customer conversations or emerging trend signals.
Source or reuse products already sold in other niches rather than inventing new ones.
Reposition them as exclusively for that avatar through branding and naming.
Create advertising and marketing only for that avatar, consistent with the rest of the funnel being tailored to it.
The source's example: rather than competing on cornhole boards, be the first cornhole clothing, supplement or energy brand.
caveats: Exclusivity claims should be truthful relative to the actual product.
The source presents this as a strategic approach, not a demonstrated performance result.
cards.source_name: How to create avatars that scale Facebook Ads to $30k days.docx
